strengths: Significance: Persistent covert channels in fine-tuned LLMs are a relevant security problem. Separating payload recovery from detecting suspicious behavior is useful, and studying both attacks and internal detection signals gives the paper a coherent research objective.

Empirical contribution: Table 1 evaluates two model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, two training datasets, and a 70B model. Several improvements over parity bucketing are substantial, including 24% to 43% exact recovery for Ministral-8B LoRA and 9% to 19% for Llama-70B. Table 2 usefully exposes strong dependence on prompt distribution rather than reporting only favorable in-distribution results.

Originality: Applying embedding-derived partitions to training-time steganography is a plausible extension of existing methods. The late-layer probe results provide an interesting observation about how secret information becomes accessible after steganographic fine-tuning, although they do not yet establish a reliable detector.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The manuscript is generally well organized, with helpful diagrams and appendices describing training configurations and probe architectures. It acknowledges degraded performance in some settings, white-box access requirements, and potential adaptive evasion. The impact statement recognizes dual-use risks and proposes detection-code release and coordinated disclosure.
weaknesses: Soundness—recoverability is not convincingly established. The proposed bucket assignment is a linear threshold in the original embedding space, but Appendix C reduces embeddings to 50 principal components before classification. This can discard precisely the random projection direction defining the labels. No linear classifier on full embeddings or sample-complexity curve is provided. Poor performance by these restricted classifiers therefore does not establish that the bucket rule is intrinsically difficult to infer. Definition 3.1 also leaves the analyst's labeled-data access and sample budget unspecified; an empirical classifier maximum is not an upper bound on recoverability.

Soundness—the KL example does not support the claimed high-capacity result. Section 7.1 assumes that the second-most-probable token, with probability 0.3, is the target and then applies its approximately 0.026-nat promotion cost to 1,024 uniformly selected buckets. That token belongs to only one bucket; the other target buckets require different, generally lower-probability tokens. Appendix B.1 likewise replaces bucket-dependent costs with a single log(alpha) in its expectation calculation. The fixed-target optimization is useful, but the stated numerical conclusion about ten bits per token does not follow.

Soundness—the perplexity result is overinterpreted and mismatched to evaluation. Theorem 7.2 concerns Q's probability of the base model's greedy token, whereas Appendix E evaluates fine-tuned generated text under the base model. A lower bound approaching two does not imply that actual models' perplexity approaches two. Even an attainable construction for the theorem's particular metric would not establish normal text quality or defeat output-based steganalysis. The broader claim that traditional detection is ineffective needs matched benign fine-tuning controls and actual detector evaluations.

Soundness—the XOR control is not proven non-decodable. Appendix G argues that needing S to compute k(S) creates a circularity that guarantees non-decodability. However, S maps deterministically to Encode(S) XOR k(S); such a map can remain injective or preserve substantial information. The finite secret space permits assessing this directly through collisions and conditional uncertainty. Without that analysis, the experiment does not establish detection in the absence of output-decodable information.

Detection validity: Sections 7.3–7.4 compare maliciously fine-tuned models only against base models. They do not establish specificity against benign fine-tuning, ordinary secret retention, or legitimate tasks requiring attention to prompt information. Secret-prediction accuracy and embedding cosine similarity are not model-level detection accuracy; no operating threshold, false-positive rate, or held-out-model evaluation is reported. Appendix F also trains and tests probes on splits drawn from the same five prompts, so the OOD designation concerns attack training, not probe generalization to unseen prompt families.

Evaluation and significance: The geometric explanation lacks controls for random balanced partitions and random collision-free letter codes, which would help separate embedding geometry from coding and partition effects. Text-quality evidence is limited to 10 prompts for coherence/stability and 20 for KL, without a direct task-utility evaluation or matched benign fine-tuning distribution. Figure 4 does not show the base-model reference supporting the claimed comparable quality. Appendix E also appears to compare distributions along separately generated prefixes, potentially confounding model drift with context differences.

Reproducibility and precision: Appendix C omits classifier dataset sizes and important optimization settings, and does not clearly specify whether secret accuracy is per-letter or exact-string accuracy. Only one bucket seed is documented, leaving robustness to partition choice unresolved. Main-result uncertainty is not clearly separated into evaluation-sample variation and independent training variation. These omissions are especially consequential because the central conclusions depend on classifier strength and seed-dependent geometry. Overall, the empirical merits do not outweigh the unresolved problems in the recoverability, theoretical, and detection claims.

strengths: Significance: Persistent secret exfiltration through fine-tuned models is an important security problem. Separating successful transmission, unauthorized payload recovery, and detection provides a useful conceptual framework.

Empirical contribution: Table 1 reports meaningful transmission improvements across multiple models and training settings, including 24% to 43% for Ministral-8B LoRA and 9% to 19% for Llama-70B LoRA. The encoding/bucketing combinations and cross-distribution evaluation help identify where improvements occur.

Originality: Applying embedding geometry to both secret encoding and vocabulary partitioning is a useful extension of TrojanStego. The late-layer probing results provide an interesting observation about representations learned during steganographic fine-tuning.

Presentation and responsible reporting: The manuscript is generally readable, provides substantial implementation details, and acknowledges unsuccessful configurations, hidden-state access requirements, and possible adaptive evasion. The impact statement recognizes dual-use risks and proposes responsible disclosure.
weaknesses: Soundness—recoverability: The central low-recoverability claim is not established by the tested classifiers. Bucket membership is explicitly a linear threshold of the original token embedding, but Appendix C reduces embeddings to only 50 principal components before classification, potentially discarding the defining direction. A full-dimensional linear classifier is an essential missing baseline. Learning the decision boundary does not require recovering its random seed. Poor performance by these restricted classifiers therefore does not establish inherent reverse-engineering difficulty.

Soundness—theoretical justification: The 10-bits-per-token example in Section 7.1 treats the second-most-probable token, with probability 0.3, as the required token across uniformly sampled buckets. That token belongs to only one of the 1,024 buckets; the remaining target buckets generally require lower-probability tokens and different pooling costs. Appendix B.1 similarly replaces bucket-dependent quantities with a single log-alpha in its expectation calculation. Consequently, the claimed expected KL of approximately 0.026 nats does not follow.

Soundness—perplexity interpretation: Theorem 7.2 concerns predicting the base model's argmax token under Q, whereas Appendix E evaluates fine-tuned generations under the base model. Its relaxed construction also allows substantial probability outside the required bucket. This does not establish low perplexity for the evaluated channel, and a lower bound approaching two does not imply actual perplexity approaches two. The theoretical results therefore do not support the broad dismissal of output-level steganalysis.

Detection validity: The probes compare maliciously fine-tuned models with base models, without matched benign fine-tuning controls. Increased accessibility of a plaintext prompt secret could reflect ordinary fine-tuning or enhanced retention of prompt information. There are no detector operating thresholds, false-positive rates, or evaluations on held-out benign and malicious models. The experiments establish a representational difference, not a reliable malicious-fine-tuning detector. This is especially consequential because benign distribution shift is the paper's stated objection to conventional detection.

Soundness—XOR control: Appendix G claims that dependence of k(S) on S ensures non-decodability. However, b XOR k(S) is simply another deterministic mapping of a finite secret space. Circular dependence alone proves neither non-invertibility nor removal of information; collision analysis or an appropriate security argument is needed. Thus the control does not establish detection in the absence of output-decodable information.

Evaluation and significance: Claims of preserved utility and distribution shifts within normal fine-tuning ranges lack matched benign controls. Coherence and stability use only 10 prompts, and KL uses 20; these proxies do not establish instruction-following quality or successful summarization. The geometry-specific explanation also needs a random balanced bucketing baseline and stronger controls. The observed transmission gains remain useful, but their mechanism and practical stealth are insufficiently supported.

Reproducibility and presentation: Although training settings are fairly detailed, Appendix C omits classifier dataset sizes and important optimization settings, and the manuscript does not clearly distinguish exact-secret accuracy from averaged letter accuracy for Rsecret. The source of uncertainty in several results is unclear, and executable detection code is promised rather than supplied in the manuscript. Overall, the useful empirical improvements do not outweigh unresolved problems in the central recoverability, theoretical, and detection claims.

strengths: Significance: Persistent covert channels introduced through fine-tuning are an important security problem. Distinguishing payload recovery from detecting a compromised model is useful and motivates complementary evaluations.

Empirical contribution: Table 1 demonstrates meaningful improvements over ASCII+Parity, including 17% to 30% exact match for Llama-8B LoRA and 24% to 43% for Ministral-8B LoRA on TrojanStego prompts. The evaluation spans two model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, and a 70B model. Table 2 also documents informative differences in generalization across prompt distributions.

Originality: Applying embedding-derived partitions to a persistent training-time channel is a useful extension of prior work. The late-layer probing results provide an interesting empirical observation about how these models represent prompt secrets.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The method is generally understandable, and the appendices provide substantial training and probe configuration details. The paper acknowledges uneven generalization, white-box access requirements, and possible adaptive evasion. Its impact statement recognizes dual-use concerns and proposes responsible disclosure.
weaknesses: Soundness—low recoverability is not established against an adequate recovery baseline. The proposed bucket assignment is a linear threshold in the original token embeddings, but Appendix C reduces embeddings to only 50 principal components before classification. This can discard precisely the information defining a random hyperplane. A linear classifier on full embeddings is an essential missing baseline under the same labeled-data access. Unknown seeds do not imply that the induced boundary requires seed search. Moreover, empirical classifier accuracy is only a lower bound on the maximum in Definition 3.1; poor performance of these restricted classifiers does not establish resistance to reverse-engineering.

Soundness—the theoretical justification for dismissing distributional detection is materially flawed. In Section 7.1, the 1,024-bucket example treats the token with probability 0.3 as the required token across non-top buckets, although that token belongs to only one bucket. The remaining bucket maxima have different probabilities and costs, invalidating the reported average of approximately 0.026 nats. Appendix B.1 similarly replaces bucket-dependent costs with a common log alpha. The perplexity construction evaluates the fine-tuned distribution on base-model greedy tokens, whereas Appendix E evaluates generated steganographic text under the base model. These results do not establish that the evaluated channels carry large payloads within normal fine-tuning drift.

Soundness—probe performance is not yet evidence of a reliable steganography detector. Sections 7.3–7.4 compare compromised models with base models, without matched benign fine-tuning controls. Greater accessibility of a plaintext prompt secret could reflect ordinary adaptation or changes in information retention. The study supplies neither detection thresholds nor false-positive rates across benign models. Its central motivation is that ordinary fine-tuning confounds output statistics, but it does not test whether the proposed internal signal suffers from the same confound. Probe train/test samples also share five generic prompt templates, so being out of distribution for model fine-tuning does not demonstrate probe generalization to unseen prompt styles.

Soundness—the XOR control does not establish non-decodability. Appendix G defines a deterministic mapping from a finite secret space to masked bitstrings. Dependence of the mask on the secret does not by itself prevent inversion: candidate secrets can be mapped forward and checked, with recoverability depending on collisions and knowledge of the mapping. The argument that circularity ensures non-decodability is incorrect. Failure of the selected classifiers therefore cannot justify the claim that this control removes decodable information from outputs.

Evaluation and significance: The text-quality evidence is too limited to establish a convincing covert channel that preserves its intended task. Coherence and stability use only 10 prompts, KL uses 20, and no direct summarization or instruction-following evaluation is reported. Figure 4 does not provide matched benign fine-tuning distributions supporting the claimed normal range. Appendix E also appears to compare next-token distributions along separately generated prefixes, which confounds parameter changes with context differences.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important measurement details remain ambiguous: whether secret recoverability is per-letter or whole-secret accuracy, the recovery-classifier sample budget and full hyperparameters, how repeated payloads are scored, and whether Table 1 uncertainty includes independent training runs. Appendix F's universal 50% bit baseline is inappropriate for constant or imbalanced ASCII bit positions. The presentation repeatedly promotes restricted empirical findings into claims of unrecoverability and effective detection. The attack improvements are promising, but these unresolved issues affect the paper's central claims and prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Training-time steganographic exfiltration is a relevant security problem. Separating payload recoverability from attack success and detectability provides a useful perspective.

Originality: Applying embedding-derived vocabulary partitions to persistent steganographic fine-tuning is a meaningful extension of TrojanStego. Table 1 shows substantial improvements in several settings, including 24%→43% exact recovery for Ministral LoRA and 17%→30% for Llama LoRA on TrojanStego prompts.

Empirical scope: The evaluation includes two model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B model, alternative prompt distributions, capability benchmarks, and mixed-motive training. The finding that benign instruction data can partly restore capabilities while preserving the channel is practically useful.

Presentation and responsible reporting: The main pipeline is clearly illustrated, and the paper acknowledges substantial capability degradation, restricted payload sizes, trigger assumptions, and hidden-state access requirements. The impact statement appropriately recognizes dual use and describes responsible disclosure plans.
weaknesses: Soundness—low recoverability is not established against an appropriate decoder. Appendix C reduces token embeddings to 50 principal components before classification, although the proposed bucket rule is exactly a linear separator in the original embedding space. This preprocessing can discard the information defining the separator. A full-dimensional linear classifier, sample-efficiency curves, and token-disjoint evaluation are essential controls. Taking the maximum accuracy of a few trained classifiers provides an empirical lower bound on achievable recovery, not evidence that stronger recovery is difficult. The source and amount of supervised bucket labels are also insufficiently specified.

Soundness—the theoretical analysis does not support the broad dismissal of output-level steganalysis. Section 7.1's 10-bit example assumes that the second-most-probable token is the target while averaging over 1,024 uniformly selected buckets; that token belongs to only one bucket, so its promotion cost cannot represent the other target buckets. Appendix B.1 similarly removes the target-dependent normalization constant from the expectation without justification. Theorem 7.2 concerns scoring the base model's argmax token under Q, whereas Appendix E evaluates fine-tuned text under the base model. These different quantities cannot establish the claimed empirical perplexity behavior. Nor is there a matched benign-fine-tuning comparison supporting the assertion that the observed shifts are normal.

Soundness—probe results demonstrate increased secret accessibility, not a validated steganography detector. Sections 7.3–7.5 compare maliciously fine-tuned models primarily against base models, without benign fine-tuned controls that also process or retain prompt information. This leaves the same fine-tuning confound used to criticize distributional detection unresolved. There are no detector thresholds, false-positive rates, ROC curves, or transfer tests across independently trained models. Probes are trained and tested on splits drawn from the same five generic prompts; being OOD relative to attack training does not establish detector generalization to unseen prompts.

Soundness—the XOR control is not proven non-decodable. Appendix G argues that requiring S to compute k(S) creates circularity that ensures non-decodability. However, S↦Encode(S) XOR k(S) is simply a deterministic mapping over 456,976 possible secrets. With the mapping known, candidate enumeration can identify preimages; whether recovery is unique depends on collisions, which are not analyzed. With the mapping unknown, decoder failure still does not establish information removal. Consequently, this control does not support the claimed separation between internal detection and output-decodable information.

Evidence reliability: Table 7 reports Ministral Full E+E exact-match accuracy of 56.7% with bit accuracy of 53.1%, and 53.4% with bit accuracy of 50.0%. Under the stated definition that exact match requires every bit to be correct, exact-match accuracy cannot exceed average bit accuracy on the same samples. Its 3.1-point bit-accuracy decline also contradicts the caption's claimed maximum of 0.4 points. These inconsistencies require correction and an evaluation audit.

Reproducibility and interpretation: Although training and probe hyperparameters are provided, important details remain missing or ambiguous, including recovery-classifier dataset sizes and XGBoost settings, whether PCA is fitted exclusively on training data, and whether uncertainty reflects independent model training or only evaluation splits. Appendix C describes per-letter classification while Definition 3.1 describes secret recovery, leaving the reported accuracy unit unclear. The methods also freeze embeddings differently for parity and embedding bucketing, introducing a training confound. These gaps, together with the unsupported recovery and detection claims, outweigh the promising attack-performance results.

strengths: Significance: Persistent covert channels in fine-tuned LLMs are a relevant security problem. Distinguishing payload recovery from channel detection is useful, and the paper investigates both attack reliability and possible defensive signals.

Empirical contribution: Table 1 reports meaningful improvements from embedding-based bucketing across multiple models and training configurations, including 17%→30% exact match for Llama-8B LoRA and 24%→43% for Ministral-8B LoRA on TrojanStego prompts. The encoding/bucketing combinations help isolate which modification contributes most.

Evaluation breadth: The paper examines prompt-distribution transfer, capability degradation, mixed-motive training, sampling temperature, and retokenization. Table 3 usefully demonstrates that plausible text quality can coexist with substantial capability losses, and that mixed-motive training mitigates some of those losses.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The main method is clearly illustrated, and the appendices provide substantial training and probing details. The limitations candidly acknowledge restricted payload sizes, trigger assumptions, capability degradation, and hidden-state access. The impact statement recognizes dual-use risks and proposes responsible disclosure; these acknowledgments are appropriate.
weaknesses: Soundness—low recoverability is not established against an adequate defender. Appendix C reduces embeddings to 50 principal components before classification, although the proposed bucket boundary is linear in the original embedding space. This preprocessing can discard information needed to infer the boundary. No full-dimensional linear classifier or sample-complexity study is provided. Limited classifier success does not establish that recovering the hidden seed is necessary or that bucket inference is intrinsically difficult. Moreover, the source and quantity of defender-accessible bit labels are insufficiently specified, and per-letter classification in Appendix C is not clearly reconciled with the secret-level accuracy in Definition 3.1.

Soundness—the theoretical argument for low distributional divergence contains a material error. Section 7.1 evaluates 1,024 uniformly selected buckets as though the target token had probability 0.3 whenever the original top token is unavailable. That second-ranked token belongs to only one bucket; the other targets must come from the remaining probability mass. Appendix B.1 likewise factors out a common log(alpha), although the optimum depends on the target bucket. Consequently, the claimed expected divergence of approximately 0.026 nats for 10 bits per token is unsupported.

Soundness—the perplexity result does not justify the stated detection conclusion. Theorem 7.2 concerns Q evaluated on the base model's top token, whereas Appendix E evaluates fine-tuned outputs under the base model. Its limiting value describes the optimum of a particular argmax-constrained problem, not the perplexity of learned steganographic models or their simultaneous KL/perplexity behavior. The empirical study also lacks matched benign fine-tuning controls to establish 'normal fine-tuning ranges.' These results do not establish that traditional steganalysis is ineffective.

Detection validity: Figures 5–6 show increased secret predictability relative to base models, rather than a validated detector of malicious fine-tuning. There are no matched benign fine-tuned controls, false-positive measurements, detection thresholds, or held-out-model detection results. Benign adaptation could also change how strongly prompt information is represented. Mixed-motive models remain malicious and do not supply this missing control. Appendix F cycles five instruction prompts across the probe dataset, so being out of distribution for model fine-tuning does not establish probe generalization to unseen prompt families.

Soundness—the purported non-decodable control is not demonstrated to be non-decodable. Section 7.5 and Appendix G argue that a deterministic secret-dependent XOR mask prevents inversion because computing the mask requires the secret. This circularity is not sufficient: the composite mapping from secrets to masked strings can still be injective or otherwise invertible. The paper provides neither an information-loss argument nor a collision analysis. Reduced accuracy of the selected classifiers therefore cannot support the stronger claim that output decoding is impossible.

Reporting and reproducibility: Table 7 reports exact-match accuracy exceeding bit accuracy for Ministral Full E+E, including 56.7% versus 53.1% at temperature zero. Under the stated all-32-bits exact-match definition, exact-match accuracy cannot exceed average bit accuracy on the same examples. Its 3.1-point bit-accuracy drop also contradicts the caption's claimed maximum of 0.4 points. These inconsistencies require correction. Recoverability sample counts, several classifier hyperparameters, and the interpretation of uncertainty across training versus evaluation runs also need clarification.

Originality and overall significance: Embedding-based bucketing is a potentially useful extension of TrojanStego, with acknowledged connections to watermarking, and the internal-representation observations merit further study. However, the broader contributions claimed—low recoverability, limits of statistical detection, and reliable mechanistic detection—are not supported by the current methodology. These are central evidential problems, rather than merely limited scope, and outweigh the promising attack-side improvements.

strengths: Significance: Persistent covert channels in fine-tuned LLMs are an important security problem. Table 1 demonstrates useful improvements over TrojanStego-style parity bucketing, including exact-match gains from 17% to 30% for Llama-8B LoRA and 24% to 43% for Ministral-8B LoRA.

Originality: Applying embedding geometry to training-time steganographic bucketing is a useful extension of prior work. Separating bucket inference from secret recovery provides a potentially valuable evaluation framework.

Empirical scope: The evaluation spans two model families, full and LoRA fine-tuning, a 70B model, prompt-distribution shifts, and mixed-motive training. Measuring capability degradation alongside attack success is particularly valuable: Table 3 shows that apparently fluent outputs can conceal substantial capability losses.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The method is generally clearly explained, with substantial implementation detail in the appendices. The limitations candidly address short payloads, trigger assumptions, capability degradation, and hidden-state access. The impact statement acknowledges dual use and proposes responsible disclosure.
weaknesses: Soundness—low recoverability is not established against an appropriate classifier. Appendix C reduces token embeddings to 50 principal components before classification, although the bucket label is defined by a linear hyperplane in the original embedding space. This reduction can discard the information needed to recover the boundary. A linear classifier on full-dimensional embeddings is an essential missing baseline. Low accuracy from these restricted classifiers does not establish that recovering the seed is necessary or that the channel resists reverse-engineering.

Soundness—the theoretical argument does not establish the claimed high-capacity, low-divergence channel. Section 7.1 uses the second-most-probable token, with probability 0.3, as the target when calculating expected KL for 1,024 uniformly selected buckets. That token belongs to only one bucket; the other target buckets require different tokens and different pooling costs. Appendix B.1 likewise replaces target-dependent normalization factors with a single value when averaging. The resulting 0.026-nat example does not support the advertised ten-bit-per-token conclusion.

Soundness—the perplexity result concerns a different quantity from the empirical evaluation. Theorem 7.2 evaluates Q on the base model's greedy token, whereas Appendix E evaluates fine-tuned generations under the base model. Its lower bound approaching two does not imply that the measured perplexity approaches two, nor establish simultaneous low KL and low perplexity. Consequently, the dismissal of distribution-based steganalysis is substantially stronger than the theory supports.

Detection validity: Sections 7.3–7.5 compare maliciously fine-tuned models primarily against base models, without matched benign fine-tuning controls. Mixed-motive models still contain the malicious objective and do not supply that control. Better secret prediction from activations therefore establishes an association, not a validated detector of malicious fine-tuning. False-positive rates, detection thresholds, and transfer across held-out models or keys are missing. The probes also train and test on the same five generic prompt templates, so their OOD setting does not establish probe generalization to unseen prompt styles.

Soundness—the XOR control is not proven non-decodable. Appendix G claims that requiring S to compute k(S) creates a circularity ensuring non-decodability. However, S maps deterministically to Encode(S) XOR k(S); such a mapping can remain invertible. The small secret domain permits checking collisions and candidate consistency when the mapping is known. Failure of the selected classifiers demonstrates limited empirical recovery, not removal of output-decodable information.

Reporting and reproducibility: Table 7 reports Ministral Full E+E exact-match accuracy of 56.7% with bit accuracy of 53.1%, and 53.4% with bit accuracy of 50.0%. Under the stated all-32-bits exact-match definition, exact-match accuracy cannot exceed average bit accuracy on the same examples. Appendix C also leaves the classifier sample count and whether secret recovery is measured per letter or per complete secret unclear. These discrepancies require resolution before the security results can be reliably interpreted.

Overall assessment: The attack improvements and representation measurements are promising, but unsupported central claims about recoverability, statistical undetectability, and mechanistic detection prevent acceptance in the current form.
